title: Neurological Pathogens
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the organisms that infect the meninges, brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves: the encapsulated bacteria of meningitis, the neonatal pathogens, the two clostridial neurotoxins, the neurotropic DNA and RNA viruses, the fungi that reach the central nervous system, and the spirochetes and leprosy bacillus. Board questions usually give one decisive clue (a Gram stain, a capsule test, an exposure, a vector, or a toxin effect) and ask you to name the organism or explain the virulence factor behind the finding. The aim here is to connect each clue to the structure or mechanism that produces it, so the answer can be reasoned out rather than memorized.

connections.how: The organisms described here are the causes of the meningitis, encephalitis, abscess, and neuropathy syndromes taught in pathology.
Botulinum toxin and tetanospasmin are explained entirely by which SNARE protein they cleave and which neuron they enter.
Terminal complement deficiency, asplenia, and low CD4 counts each predict a specific set of nervous system pathogens.
CSF cell type, protein, and glucose distinguish bacterial, viral, and fungal meningitis, and basilar exudates or capsular polysaccharide raise intracranial pressure.

sections.title: The encapsulated meningitis bacteria: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and Hib

blocks.text: Three bacteria cause most community-acquired bacterial meningitis after the newborn period, and they share a route: nasopharyngeal colonization, passage across the mucosa, survival in blood, and seeding of the subarachnoid space. Survival in blood depends on a polysaccharide capsule, which limits C3b deposition and masks any bound C3b from phagocyte receptors, so the bacteria escape opsonization. Clearance then needs anticapsular antibody and the spleen, whose macrophages remove poorly opsonized bacteria, so asplenia raises the risk from all three.

Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus: alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble. Its capsule has about 100 serotypes and swells with type-specific antiserum (the quellung reaction). Pneumolysin damages ependymal and cochlear cells, IgA1 protease cleaves mucosal IgA, and autolysin releases cell wall fragments that drive inflammation. It is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults and leaves the most sequelae, including hearing loss.

Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative, kidney-bean-shaped diplococcus, oxidase positive and a fermenter of maltose as well as glucose (gonococcus ferments only glucose). Pili attach it to nasopharyngeal epithelium, and it spreads by respiratory droplets in crowded settings such as dormitories and barracks. Its capsule resists complement, and the serogroup B capsule is polysialic acid resembling host neural cell adhesion molecule, so it is poorly immunogenic. LOS shed in outer membrane blebs activates TLR4, releasing TNF and IL-1 that cause capillary leak, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpura, and adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome). Because Neisseria is killed mainly by the membrane attack complex, C5 to C9 deficiency predisposes to recurrent neisserial infection.

Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) is a small gram-negative coccobacillus needing factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD), so it grows on chocolate agar or as satellite colonies around Staphylococcus aureus. Its polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule is the main virulence factor, and anti-PRP antibody is protective. Infants respond poorly to plain polysaccharide, so before conjugate vaccines Hib meningitis was concentrated between about 6 months, when maternal IgG wanes, and 5 years (NE-18).

sections.title: Neonatal meningitis: group B Streptococcus, E. coli K1, and Listeria

blocks.text: Newborns meet a different set of organisms because their defenses are immature. Complement levels are low, neutrophil reserves and chemotaxis are limited, and antibody consists almost entirely of maternal IgG carried across the placenta, mostly in the third trimester, so preterm infants receive less. The organisms that exploit this come from the mother: from the birth canal and perineum, or across the placenta.

Streptococcus agalactiae (group B Streptococcus, GBS) is a gram-positive coccus in chains that is beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, CAMP test positive, and hippurate positive. It colonizes the vagina and rectum of a sizable minority of pregnant women. Its capsule is rich in sialic acid, which recruits the host regulator factor H and inactivates C3b on the bacterial surface, so the alternative pathway fails. An infant is protected only if the mother has transferred anticapsular IgG. Early-onset disease, in the first week and often the first day, follows aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or vaginal secretions and presents as sepsis or pneumonia; late-onset disease, from about 1 week to 3 months, more often presents as meningitis. GBS is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis.

Escherichia coli carrying the K1 capsule is the second most common cause and is especially important in preterm infants. The K1 capsule is the same polysialic acid found on meningococcus serogroup B and on host neural cell adhesion molecule, so it is poorly immunogenic and resists complement. A high-grade bacteremia is followed by invasion of brain microvascular endothelial cells, which carries the organism into the CSF.

Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod (sometimes mistaken for a diphtheroid contaminant) that is catalase positive, narrowly beta-hemolytic, and shows tumbling motility at room temperature. It grows at refrigerator temperature, about 4 °C (39 °F), so cold storage enriches it in deli meats, soft cheeses, and unpasteurized milk. It is a facultative intracellular organism that spends its life inside host cells, out of reach of antibody. Clearance therefore needs cell-mediated immunity (Th1 cells, interferon gamma-activated macrophages, and CD8 T cells), which is why neonates, pregnant women, older adults, and people on corticosteroids or transplant immunosuppression are at risk. Internalin binds E-cadherin, which helps Listeria cross the intestinal epithelium and the placenta, leading to amnionitis, fetal loss, or disseminated granulomas in the newborn (granulomatosis infantiseptica). In adults it can cause rhombencephalitis, an infection of the brainstem.

blocks.text: Transmitter release requires the SNARE proteins. Synaptobrevin on the vesicle zips with syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the plasma membrane to dock it, and when Ca2+ enters through voltage-gated channels and binds synaptotagmin, the vesicle fuses and releases its contents. Botulinum toxin and tetanospasmin are closely related AB toxins: the heavy chain binds gangliosides and protein receptors on the nerve terminal and mediates entry, and the light chain is a zinc endopeptidase that cleaves a SNARE protein. Their opposite clinical pictures come from which neuron they end up in, not from a different molecular action. Binding is irreversible, so function returns only as new terminals and SNAREs are made over weeks to months.

Clostridium botulinum is an anaerobic, spore-forming gram-positive rod. Of its serotypes (A to G), A, B, and E cause most human disease; A and E cleave SNAP-25 and B cleaves synaptobrevin. Toxin absorbed into the blood acts at peripheral cholinergic terminals: the neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia, and parasympathetic endings. It does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so consciousness and sensation are preserved. Weakness is symmetric and descending, beginning with cranial nerve muscles (diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia) and spreading to the limbs and diaphragm, without fever. Cholinergic autonomic failure adds dilated, poorly reactive pupils, dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention. Adults usually ingest preformed toxin in home-canned low-acid food; the toxin is heat labile but the spores are heat resistant. In infant botulism, spores (classically from honey) germinate in a gut that lacks mature flora and make toxin there, giving constipation and a floppy baby. Wound botulism follows contaminated wounds, including injection drug use.

Clostridium tetani is an anaerobic gram-positive rod with a terminal spore. Spores in soil enter puncture or necrotic wounds, where low oxygen lets them germinate. Tetanospasmin enters motor nerve terminals but is sorted into retrograde transport, carried to motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord and brainstem, and passed across the synapse into the inhibitory interneurons that synapse on them, including Renshaw cells. There it cleaves synaptobrevin, stopping release of glycine and GABA. Motor neurons lose their brake and reciprocal inhibition fails, so agonist and antagonist muscles contract together: trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonos as the stronger back extensors win, and painful generalized spasms triggered by stimuli, with the patient awake. Loss of inhibition of sympathetic neurons causes autonomic instability. Neonatal tetanus follows infection of the umbilical stump.

blocks.explain: Dilated pupils with descending flaccid weakness means acetylcholine release has failed at peripheral cholinergic terminals; trismus and opisthotonos mean inhibitory interneurons in the cord have been silenced.

sections.title: DNA viruses of the nervous system: herpesviruses and JC polyomavirus

blocks.text: Both groups of DNA viruses that matter in the nervous system persist for life after the first infection, and both cause neurological disease mainly when they come out of latency. They differ in where they hide and in what they damage.

Herpesviruses are enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus and take their envelope from nuclear and Golgi membranes. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV) enter at epithelial surfaces, infect the sensory nerve endings beneath, and travel by retrograde axonal transport to the sensory ganglion. There the genome circularizes and persists as an episome in the neuronal nucleus, with transcription limited mainly to latency-associated transcripts and no infectious virus made, so the neuron displays little viral antigen to cytotoxic T cells. Reactivation, provoked by fever, ultraviolet light, stress, or falling cell-mediated immunity, sends virus by anterograde transport back down the axon to the skin or mucosa supplied by that neuron, which is why lesions recur in the same place and, for VZV, in a single dermatome.

HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion and is the leading cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis, with a characteristic preference for the medial temporal and orbitofrontal lobes. The result is a hemorrhagic necrotizing encephalitis that produces fever, personality change, aphasia, olfactory or gustatory hallucinations, and temporal lobe seizures, with red cells and raised protein in a lymphocytic CSF; nuclear Cowdry A inclusions may be seen. HSV-2 is latent in sacral ganglia, causes recurrent genital lesions and benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis, and causes severe disseminated or meningoencephalitic disease in neonates infected during vaginal delivery. VZV causes chickenpox on first infection, then persists in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia; reactivation gives dermatomal zoster, and because inflammation damages the ganglion and dorsal root it can leave postherpetic neuralgia. Reactivation in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve threatens the eye, and in the geniculate ganglion it causes facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). VZV can also cause a granulomatous vasculitis with stroke.

JC polyomavirus is a small nonenveloped virus with a circular double-stranded DNA genome. Most adults are infected silently in childhood and carry it latently in kidney tubular epithelium and lymphoid tissue. When cellular immunity fails, as in untreated HIV with a low CD4 count, hematologic malignancy, or therapy that blocks lymphocyte trafficking into the brain, the virus reaches the brain and infects oligodendrocytes. Because each oligodendrocyte myelinates many axons, lysis of these cells produces progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML): patchy, asymmetric demyelination of subcortical white matter with enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei containing inclusions, bizarre reactive astrocytes, and little inflammation. Clinically it gives subacute, stepwise focal deficits such as hemiparesis, visual field loss, ataxia, and cognitive decline, with nonenhancing white matter lesions that spare the cortex.

sections.title: RNA viruses of the nervous system: enteroviruses, West Nile virus, and rabies

blocks.text: RNA viruses reach the nervous system by one of two routes. Most arrive through the blood after replicating elsewhere, so they need a viremia high enough and long enough to cross the blood-brain barrier or choroid plexus. Rabies is the exception, travelling inside peripheral nerves instead.

Enteroviruses (poliovirus, coxsackieviruses A and B, echoviruses, and enterovirus 71) are nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA picornaviruses. Lacking an envelope, they tolerate stomach acid, bile, and detergents, which allows fecal-oral spread and makes them the most common cause of aseptic meningitis, typically in summer and early autumn. They replicate in pharyngeal and intestinal lymphoid tissue, then spread through the blood to the meninges, causing a self-limited lymphocytic meningitis. Poliovirus is tropic for anterior horn motor neurons and brainstem motor nuclei; destroying those cell bodies gives asymmetric flaccid paralysis with areflexia, wasting, and no sensory loss, because only the lower motor neuron is lost.

West Nile virus is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA flavivirus maintained between birds and Culex mosquitoes; humans and horses are dead-end hosts whose viremia is too low to infect a feeding mosquito. Most infections are silent or febrile only; neuroinvasive disease is far more likely in older adults and the immunosuppressed, because control depends on early interferon and antibody responses. It causes meningitis, encephalitis with tremor and parkinsonian features, and a poliomyelitis-like asymmetric flaccid paralysis from infection of anterior horn cells.

Rabies virus is an enveloped, bullet-shaped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA rhabdovirus, so it carries its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. US reservoirs are bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes; worldwide, dog bites dominate. It replicates in muscle, binds receptors at the neuromuscular junction including the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, then moves by dynein-driven retrograde transport to the dorsal root ganglion, cord, and brain. Because transport is slow and the virus stays shielded inside the axon, incubation is long and variable, typically one to three months and shorter for bites on the face and neck than on a distal limb, and little antigen is seen until the virus is central. Encephalitis follows, with agitation, hydrophobia, autonomic storms, then paralysis, coma, and death; about one fifth of cases take a paralytic form. Eosinophilic cytoplasmic Negri bodies appear in cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal neurons. Centrifugal spread along nerves then puts virus in saliva.

blocks.title: Worked example: two causes of flaccid paralysis
blocks.text: A previously well child develops fever, then asymmetric weakness of one leg with absent reflexes, wasting, and normal sensation. A 78-year-old man in late summer develops fever, confusion, tremor, and asymmetric arm weakness with areflexia. Both pictures localize to the anterior horn, because loss of the lower motor neuron gives flaccid weakness, areflexia, and atrophy without sensory loss. Age, season, and mosquito exposure favor West Nile virus in the older man, while an unimmunized child with fecal-oral exposure favors poliovirus. Botulinum toxin would also give flaccid weakness, but it is symmetric, descending, and accompanied by dilated pupils rather than fever and asymmetry.

sections.title: Fungi that reach the nervous system

blocks.text: Fungi reach the nervous system through the blood after inhalation or by direct invasion from the sinuses. Which fungus causes disease depends less on exposure, which is common, than on which host defense has failed: neutrophils handle hyphae, so neutropenia favors invasive molds, while T cells and macrophages contain yeasts and spherules, so a low CD4 count favors Cryptococcus.

Cryptococcus neoformans is a narrow-based budding yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule of glucuronoxylomannan. It lives in soil enriched with pigeon droppings. Inhaled yeast reaches the alveoli, where macrophages and CD4 T cells normally contain it; when CD4 counts fall below about 100 cells per microliter it disseminates, with marked tropism for the central nervous system, where little complement or antibody is present to oppose the capsule. The capsule blocks phagocytosis, sheds soluble antigen, and obstructs CSF outflow so pressure rises. The result is a subacute meningoencephalitis with headache, fever, and little neck stiffness, because the capsule provokes weak inflammation, plus cranial nerve palsies and visual loss from high pressure. India ink shows a clear halo because the capsule excludes the ink, and the capsular antigen test on CSF or serum is the most sensitive marker. Gelatinous pseudocysts along perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia give the soap-bubble appearance.

Mucor and Rhizopus, in the order Mucorales, grow as broad, ribbon-like hyphae that are nonseptate (or sparsely septate) and branch at wide, nearly right angles. They are angioinvasive: they penetrate arterial walls, causing thrombosis and bloodless necrosis of the tissue downstream. Diabetic ketoacidosis is the classic setting because acidemia releases iron from transferrin, giving the fungus free iron that its siderophores capture, while hyperglycemia and ketones support growth and impair neutrophil function. Infection begins in the nose and paranasal sinuses and extends into the orbit, then through the cribriform plate or orbital apex into the frontal lobe and cavernous sinus, giving facial pain, orbital swelling, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, and a black necrotic eschar on the palate or turbinate. Iron overload, neutropenia, and transplant immunosuppression are the other settings. Aspergillus, by contrast, has narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles and usually arrives from the lung.

Coccidioides is a dimorphic fungus of dry soil in the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Latin America. Soil disruption by wind or construction aerosolizes arthroconidia, which are inhaled and convert in the lung into thick-walled spherules packed with endospores; when a spherule ruptures, each endospore forms a new spherule, so one inhaled particle multiplies locally. Most infections are a self-limited pneumonia (Valley fever) with erythema nodosum and eosinophilia. Dissemination to skin, bone, and meninges is far more likely with defective cellular immunity, and also in pregnancy. Coccidioidal meningitis is chronic and basilar: granulomatous exudate at the base of the brain obstructs CSF flow, causing hydrocephalus and cranial nerve palsies, with lymphocytic CSF, low glucose, and high protein.

blocks.predict: Why does cryptococcal meningitis cause severe headache and visual loss with only mild neck stiffness, while coccidioidal meningitis causes hydrocephalus?

blocks.text: These three organisms damage nerves slowly, over weeks to years, and all are hard to see or to grow.

Treponema pallidum is a thin, tightly coiled spirochete about 0.2 micrometers wide, below the resolution of ordinary light microscopy, so it is found by darkfield examination of fresh exudate, by silver or immunofluorescent stain in tissue, or by serology; it cannot be grown on artificial media. Its outer membrane has very few surface proteins, giving antibody few targets. It spreads through blood and lymph within hours, so even the primary chancre is systemic disease, and it enters the nervous system early.

Serology uses two classes of test. Nontreponemal tests (VDRL and RPR) detect antibody to a cardiolipin antigen released from damaged host cells; titers follow disease activity, and biologic false positives occur in pregnancy, lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and viral infections. Treponemal tests (FTA-ABS and newer immunoassays) detect antibody to the organism and stay positive for life.

Neurosyphilis takes several forms: early meningitis, meningovascular syphilis with endarteritis and stroke, and late parenchymal disease. Tabes dorsalis is degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots, with lightning pains, sensory ataxia, areflexia, and loss of position and vibration sense; general paresis is cortical neuronal loss with dementia and personality change. The Argyll Robertson pupil accommodates but does not react to light.

Borrelia burgdorferi is a larger, loosely coiled spirochete visible with Giemsa stain, transmitted by Ixodes ticks; nymphs feed on white-footed mice, the reservoir, and adults on deer, which sustain the tick population but are not a reservoir for the bacterium. Transmission usually needs prolonged attachment. It spreads outward in the skin as erythema migrans, then disseminates, varying its surface lipoproteins and binding host complement regulators so it persists while antibody accumulates. Neurologic disease, often weeks after the bite, combines lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathy (most often facial palsy), and painful radiculoneuritis; carditis with AV block belongs to the same stage, and late disease brings arthritis. Antibody takes weeks to appear, so early serology can be negative.

Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast bacillus that cannot be cultured in vitro, grown only in armadillos or mouse footpads; wild armadillos are a US reservoir. It grows best at about 30 °C (86 °F), below core temperature, so it colonizes cooler tissue: skin, nasal mucosa, anterior eye, and superficial nerves. It is an obligate intracellular organism that binds laminin-2 in the Schwann cell basal lamina, and infection plus the immune response destroys the nerve. Because damage follows superficial nerve trunks, sensory loss is patchy or follows a thickened palpable nerve rather than a dermatome, and loss of pain leads to unnoticed injury and loss of digits. The T cell response sets the form: strong Th1 gives tuberculoid leprosy with few organisms, granulomas, and a few sharply bordered anesthetic patches, while weak Th1 with dominant Th2 gives lepromatous leprosy with abundant bacilli in foamy macrophages, diffuse symmetric skin thickening, and widespread nerve involvement.

integration.text: Anatomy and immunology together predict which organism a given patient will get. The capsule is the central theme of extracellular bacterial and cryptococcal disease, so the defenses that handle capsules (anticapsular antibody, complement, and the spleen) define the risk groups: asplenia for all three capsular meningitis bacteria, terminal complement deficiency for Neisseria, and infancy for any plain polysaccharide, which is why conjugation to a protein carrier matters (NE-18). Intracellular organisms invert the logic: Listeria, Mycobacterium leprae, JC virus, Cryptococcus, and Coccidioides become dangerous when T cells and macrophages fail, which is why pregnancy, corticosteroids, transplant immunosuppression, and a low CD4 count select for them. Route explains the rest. Organisms that travel inside axons (rabies virus, herpesviruses, and tetanospasmin) bypass antibody entirely, which gives rabies its long silent incubation and herpesviruses their lifelong latency, while organisms that depend on viremia are limited by interferon and antibody responses that weaken with age.

Pathology and physiology explain the findings used to identify these infections. Neutrophil influx with bacterial cell wall products gives the high-protein, low-glucose, neutrophilic CSF of pyogenic meningitis, while lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose points to a virus, and lymphocytic CSF with low glucose points to a fungus or mycobacterium. Mechanical and vascular consequences follow structure: the cryptococcal capsule and the coccidioidal basilar exudate obstruct CSF outflow and raise pressure, Mucorales hyphae invade arteries and cause ischemic necrosis, and treponemal endarteritis causes stroke in a young adult. There are limits to this reasoning. Clinical pictures overlap widely, several organisms cause the same syndrome in the same host, and identification rests on stain, antigen, serology, or nucleic acid testing rather than on pattern alone; serologic tests also carry their own false positives and false negatives, which is why nontreponemal and treponemal syphilis tests are interpreted together.

summary: The capsule is the shared virulence factor of S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Hib, group B Streptococcus, E. coli K1, and Cryptococcus: it blocks opsonization and phagocytosis.
Meningococcal LOS drives shock, DIC, purpura, and adrenal hemorrhage; terminal complement deficiency predisposes specifically to Neisseria because killing needs the membrane attack complex.
In neonatal CSF, gram-positive cocci in chains mean group B Streptococcus, gram-negative rods mean E. coli K1, and gram-positive rods mean Listeria.
Listeria lives in the cytosol and moves cell to cell on actin tails, so clearance requires cell-mediated immunity, which explains the risk in pregnancy, infancy, age, and immunosuppression.

Botulinum toxin and tetanospasmin are both zinc proteases that cleave SNARE proteins; botulinum blocks acetylcholine peripherally for flaccid descending weakness, while tetanospasmin is carried retrograde to block glycine and GABA for spastic paralysis.
Herpesviruses are latent in sensory ganglia and move along axons in both directions; JC virus is latent in the kidney and lyses oligodendrocytes to produce PML.

Enteroviruses are nonenveloped and spread fecal-oral as the leading cause of aseptic meningitis, and poliovirus and West Nile virus both destroy anterior horn cells to give asymmetric flaccid paralysis without sensory loss.
Rabies travels retrograde inside axons, so incubation is long and depends on the distance from bite to brain, and Negri bodies appear in Purkinje and hippocampal neurons.

Cryptococcus gives high-pressure meningitis detected by capsular antigen and an India ink halo; Mucorales invade vessels from the sinus in ketoacidosis because acidemia frees iron; Coccidioides forms spherules and a chronic basilar meningitis with hydrocephalus.

Nontreponemal titers follow syphilis activity but give false positives, treponemal tests stay positive for life, Borrelia causes meningitis with facial palsy and radiculoneuritis, and M. leprae infects Schwann cells in cool superficial nerves.

verify: Reference CSF values (protein about 15 to 45 mg/dL, glucose about 60% of plasma, opening pressure about 10 to 20 cm H2O) vary slightly by source and by laboratory; confirm the ranges NABNE uses.
Rates of maternal group B Streptococcus colonization and the relative frequency of neonatal meningitis pathogens differ by region and era; this chapter gives the order rather than percentages.
The CD4 threshold for cryptococcal disease (below about 100 cells per microliter) is a commonly cited figure; some sources use below 200.
Optimal growth temperature for M. leprae is given as about 30 °C (86 °F) in some texts and as a range of about 27 to 30 °C (81 to 86 °F) in others.
The proportion of rabies cases that take the paralytic form (about 20%) and the usual incubation range (about one to three months) are consensus approximations.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Waterhouse-Friderichsen, Ramsay Hunt, Argyll Robertson, Negri body, Cowdry A inclusion, and granulomatosis infantiseptica, or only descriptive terms.
